sections.text: A struct groups related values under one name. Each value is a field with its own name and type.
Read a field with a dot: p.name. To change fields, the whole variable must be mut:
Add #[derive(Debug)] above a struct to print it with {:?}, or {:#?} for a tidy multi-line view:
A struct is like a form with labelled boxes: every Player has a name box, a level box and an online box.

Rust has no classes or inheritance. Data lives in structs and enums, behaviour goes in impl blocks (next lesson), and shared behaviour comes from traits. Tuple structs like struct Meters(f64); give a plain value its own type.

exercise.prompt: Finish make_book so it creates a Book with the given title and pages. For make_book("Dune", 412), main should print: Dune has 412 pages

tests.label: make_book("Dune", 412) keeps the title and the pages
The program prints Dune has 412 pages
values a hard-coded Dune would not match

hints: Look at how the struct is defined, then create a value with a field for each piece of data. That Book is the value the function returns.
Create it like this: Book { title: ..., pages: ... }. The title field is a String, but the parameter is a &str, so write String::from(title). Read fields with book.title.
Replace the let _ line and todo!() with Book { title: String::from(title), pages: pages } and no semicolon, so it is the value the function returns.
